summary: Defines a MIME header, Content-features, that annotates a message part with a media feature expression describing what is needed to handle it. It also suggests some ways to use that header.

eli5.summary: A letter can carry a note saying what is needed to view it, like color or screen size. This defines the label for that note in email.

questions: what is a media feature in mime
how does content-features work with multipart
subtitle: A MIME header that labels a message part with the media features needed to handle it.

tldr.problem: The MIME Content-type header says little about what a message part needs in order to be shown properly, and says nothing useful about encrypted, zipped or externally referenced content.
tldr.mechanism: A new Content-features header carries a media feature expression, written in the format of RFC 2533, that describes the content of a message part.
tldr.outcome: Agents can learn about a message's media features without opening it, but the header is not protected inside signed data and can leak information about encrypted content.

today: RFC 2912 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2000, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the expression format of RFC 2533.

sections.title: Introduction and Terms
sections.content:
RFC 2533 defines a format for describing media feature capabilities as a combination of simple media feature tags, registered under the procedure in RFC 2506. RFC 2912 defines a MIME Content-features: header that uses these expressions to annotate a message part.

A media feature is information about the facilities assumed to be available for the content to be properly rendered or presented. It does not include information that affects message transmission. A feature set expression is a string that describes some set of features, written under the rules of RFC 2533. The RFC uses the ABNF notation of RFC 2234.
sections.eli5: A media feature is something you need to look at a message properly, like a color screen. The sticker lists what is needed.

sections.title: Motivation and Goals
sections.content:
The RFC lists four ways the labelling is expected to be used.

  • To give more detail about the content than the Content-type: header can.
  • To summarize the content of a composite part, such as a multipart or message, without opening the inner content.
  • To describe external data referenced by a part, for example a message/external-body, which cannot be found by examining the message.
  • To describe content that is encrypted or held in an application-specific file structure that hides it from a MIME processor.
sections.eli5: The sticker is handy when you cannot peek inside the box, because it is sealed, locked or still on a faraway shelf.

sections.title: The Content-features Header
sections.content:
The RFC extends the optional-field syntax of RFC 822 with Content-features followed by a Feature-expr. That is simply the filter expression from section 4.1 of RFC 2533. The header gives extra information about the content directly contained in, or indirectly referenced by, the MIME part.

Feature expressions can be very long. RFC 2533 allows whitespace between the elements of an expression, and RFC 822 and MIME allow headers to be folded where whitespace appears. The RFC therefore recommends including whitespace, especially in long expressions, so that agents that do not understand the field can still fold it.
sections.eli5: The sticker is written in a special short-hand. If it is long, you can break it into lines at the spaces.

sections.title: How to Use It on Different Parts
sections.content:
On a simple part, the header should appear just once. It may name a content type that differs from Content-type:, which is possible but not recommended for a non-composite part. MIME content type processing must always follow the Content-type: header.

On a multipart or other composite, headers describe the inner content. Implementations must not assume one header per body part: headers may be in a different order than the parts, one header may cover several parts, and several headers may cover one part. To tie features to a specific part, the header should be put on that part itself. The same applies to opaque composites such as application/zip or an encrypted message.

For external data, one or more headers can describe the referenced data, including its MIME content types, for example for a message/external-body.
sections.eli5: On a single item the sticker says a bit more about it. On a box of many items, the stickers are a rough summary, so for exact details put a sticker on each item.

sections.title: Examples from the RFC
sections.content:
The RFC gives six examples. A simple text message carries (& (paper-size=A4) (ua-media=stationery) ). A fax message wraps TIFF images in a multipart/mixed and lists features such as dpi=200, image-coding=MH and paper-size=A4 on the outer part.

In a multipart/alternative, the outer headers list the available alternatives before any are processed, which may allow one-pass processing. There may be alternatives with the same content type but different features, and there is no defined correspondence between headers and parts.

Other examples show a message/external-body pointing at a URL, a application/zip whose hidden contents are described (overcoming a problem noted in its MIME registration), and a multipart/related HTML page with a GIF image.
sections.eli5: The examples show stickers on a fax, on a box of alternatives, on a zip file and on a web page with a picture. In each case the sticker tells you what is inside without opening it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For simple or multipart MIME data, the header gives a summary that can often be found by looking at the content, so the RFC sees no extra concerns. For other composites, especially encrypted content, a feature expression may disclose information that is otherwise unavailable. Care is needed so that encryption's purpose is not compromised, for example when it is meant to hide that a particular application data format is used.

If the header is applied to a multipart/signed object, or outside any other signed data, the feature information is not protected and could be tampered with, possibly fooling implementations. Putting it inside the signed data would fix this, at the cost of requiring implementations to parse the inner structure to find it.
sections.eli5: A sticker on a locked box might give away a secret about what is in it. And anyone can swap a sticker, because it is not covered by the seal.

items.title: More detail
items.text: Goes beyond what Content-type can say.

items.title: Composite summary
items.text: Describes a multipart or message without opening it.

items.title: External data
items.text: Describes data referenced by a part, such as message/external-body.

items.title: Hidden content
items.text: Describes encrypted or opaquely structured content.
